data.title: Wall Street’s next big test is hiding in America’s shopping trolley
data.description:
Walmart and Target will report quarterly earnings next week, giving Wall Street a closer look at how American households are spending as holiday shopping gathers pace.

Shoppers face familiar choices: switch to cheaper groceries, postpone buying a household appliance or wait for a discount before purchasing gifts. Those decisions can lift sales while squeezing profit on each purchase.

Target reports on Wednesday, 18 November, followed by Walmart on Thursday, 19 November.

Investors will be watching not simply how much consumers spend, but who is spending, what goes into their baskets and how much money retailers keep.

More spending does not always mean stronger households

A larger checkout bill is not necessarily a sign of prosperity. Prices can rise while customers buy fewer products, and stronger spending by wealthy households can conceal weaker demand elsewhere.

Alvarez & Marsal's consumer survey, released on 12 November, illustrates that divide.

The consultancy surveyed over 2,000 US consumers in late August and early September, finding that higher-income households planned to spend more over the holidays while lower-income respondents expected cuts across every holiday category.

“Dollars are likely to rise with prices and affluent spending, even as most households plan to do less,” the firm's Fall 2026 Consumer Sentiment Survey concluded.

That is a forecast about shopping intentions, not a measure of purchases already made. It also helps explain why two retailers reporting growing sales might be serving very different customers.

The survey found that 49% of respondents wait for promotional events such as Black Friday or Cyber Monday, at least for big-ticket items.

Among shoppers trying to reduce grocery expenditure, 39% planned to switch to cheaper brands within their usual store.

The same shopper poses different tests for Walmart and Target

Walmart's previous quarter offered one useful starting point. US comparable sales excluding fuel increased 2.6%, supported by 1.5% more transactions and a 1.1% higher average ticket.

The question next week is whether customers keep visiting and add toys, clothing and other discretionary goods alongside everyday essentials.

Target's latest comparable sales grew 3.8%, driven mainly by a 3.6% rise in traffic rather than substantially bigger baskets.

Investors will look for repeat visits, demand across its merchandise categories and evidence that promotions are driving profitable purchases.

Comparable sales broadly capture growth from established stores and relevant online sales, rather than expansion through new outlets.

Each retailer has its own definition, making traffic, ticket size and the mix of products important alongside the headline percentage.

The discount that wins a shopper can prove costly. Gross margin measures the proportion of sales remaining after the cost of merchandise.

Aggressive markdowns might bring customers through the door while leaving less profit behind, particularly if retailers also carry excess inventory.

“Consumers are making discretionary trade-offs and starting their holiday shopping earlier,” said Mark Chambers, EY Americas retail sector leader.

Early promotions might encourage additional purchases. Equally, they could simply pull December spending into November, making holiday sales difficult to interpret until the full season has passed.

Walmart and Target therefore face a shared test of profitability, not an identical test of demand. Walmart needs to show that its value proposition produces earnings growth.

Target must demonstrate that more visits and appealing offers translate into sustainable margins.

A resilient consumer can still disappoint Wall Street

Caution does not mean Americans have stopped shopping.

“People express frustration and anger and disappointment — and then they go out and shop,” Eric Fisch, HSBC's US head of retail and apparel, told Vogue Business.

That gap between mood and behaviour helps explain the National Retail Federation's October forecast: holiday sales would rise 4.2% to $1.013 trillion during November and December.

The estimate excludes automobile dealers, petrol stations and restaurants, and concerns dollar sales, not the number of items bought.

Nor is every purchase an endorsement of a retailer's pricing power.

Shoppers might spend on food and seasonal necessities while delaying furniture or electronics, or buy premium gifts only after sacrificing everyday extras. Changing categories can matter as much as the total bill.

Stock investors face expectations. A retailer could deliver solid growth yet disappoint if its share price already anticipates stronger results.

Another could rally on modest improvement if investors had feared worse.

Next week's earnings will provide clues through comparable sales, transaction counts, gross margins, inventory and holiday guidance.

Management comments on promotions will matter especially: are retailers winning additional business, or paying too much to secure it?

data.title: Evening digest: oil heads for weekly decline, Tesla SpaceX merger talks advance
data.description:
Oil prices edged higher on Friday as signs of a growing global supply surplus and easing concerns over further military escalation in the Middle East weighed on the market.

Meanwhile, US producer inflation rose less than expected in October, although persistent price pressures continued to complicate the Federal Reserve's policy outlook.

Oil prices head for second weekly decline

Oil prices gained on Friday; however, Brent and West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude are on track for a second consecutive weekly decline.

Brent futures fell 0.13% to $95.94 a barrel, while WTI declined 0.09% to $88.81.

Both benchmarks were set to lose around 2% for the week, following declines of 16% and 13%, respectively, in the previous week.

The market has shifted from concerns about supply shortages to fears of a potential surplus.

An International Energy Agency report released on Friday pointed to an increase in the global oil surplus, while lower geopolitical risks also weighed on prices.

US crude and fuel inventories also increased last week, reflecting softer demand for refined products and higher oil imports, according to the Energy Information Administration.

However, risks to shipments through the Strait of Hormuz remain.

Iran's military said four oil tankers were hit by explosions in the waterway on Thursday, while Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis claimed attacks on Saudi oil infrastructure.

US PPI rises less than expected in October

US wholesale prices increased 0.3% in October, below the 0.4% forecast by economists surveyed by Dow Jones, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics.

Core PPI, which excludes food and energy, also rose 0.3%, in line with expectations.

However, the annual headline rate accelerated to 6.5%, its highest level since November 2022.

Goods prices were a major contributor to the increase.

Final demand goods prices rose 0.5% during the month, while the goods index increased 10.2% year over year, its largest annual gain since October 2022.

Services prices rose 0.2%, with transportation and warehousing contributing to the increase. Truck freight transportation prices climbed 3.9%.

The figures offered some relief after consumer inflation also came in hotter than expected earlier in the week.

However, the annual acceleration in producer prices and broader cost pressures could complicate the Fed's next decision.

Markets were pricing in a December rate increase, with the CME FedWatch tool showing an 87.7% probability of a 25-basis-point hike and a 12.3% chance of a 50-basis-point move.

Gold struggles despite softer PPI reading

Gold prices fell on Friday after the producer inflation report came in below expectations.

However, the modest recovery did little to offset the previous session's steep losses.

Spot gold fell 0.03% to $3,875.14 an ounce, after briefly reaching $3,922.97 following the PPI release. US gold futures for December delivery fell 0.14% to 3,880.10.

Bullion fell 3% on Thursday, reaching a more-than-one-year low as higher oil prices and hotter-than-expected consumer inflation strengthened concerns about interest rates remaining elevated.

Gold was down around 4.5% for the week, putting it on course for its worst weekly performance since early June.

Higher interest rates tend to reduce the appeal of non-yielding assets such as gold. Silver and platinum also declined on Friday, while palladium advanced.

Tesla and SpaceX merger talks gather pace

Tesla and SpaceX could announce a merger as soon as December, according to a Bloomberg report published on Thursday.

The potential deal would combine Tesla's electric vehicles, energy storage and robotics businesses with SpaceX's rockets, satellites and artificial intelligence operations.

Based on their valuations of more than $1.9 trillion and around $1.5 trillion, respectively, the combined company could be worth approximately $3.4 trillion to $3.5 trillion.

Boards and advisers are reportedly discussing the terms, including the exchange ratio for Tesla shareholders and the governance structure.

An announcement could still be delayed until early 2027.

Elon Musk, who leads both companies and is their largest shareholder, has previously described a merger as a good idea, citing potential synergies in AI, chip design, robotics and orbital computing.

However, significant hurdles remain.

Tesla's China business, which accounts for roughly 20% of its revenue and a larger share of its earnings and free cash flow, could complicate the transaction.

JPMorgan has identified Chinese regulatory approval as the biggest obstacle.

Any deal would also require clearances across multiple jurisdictions and approval from Tesla shareholders, while the special committees overseeing discussions must demonstrate that their decisions serve shareholders' interests.

data.title: Nvidia stock outlook: Can shares recover after Jensen Huang's exit?
data.description:
Nvidia shares NVDA remained under pressure on Friday, falling 2.17% at the time of writing after recovering from an intraday decline of 4.6%.

The latest losses followed a 4.3% drop on Thursday after founder and longtime CEO Jensen Huang resigned amid reports concerning his personal relationships.

The departure has raised questions about Nvidia's leadership succession, corporate culture and exposure to potential regulatory scrutiny.

The company is also on track for its largest weekly market capitalisation decline on record.

However, analysts remain divided on the stock's outlook, with some arguing that its valuation offers an attractive entry point while others warn that the controversy could create longer-term risks.

Nvidia valuation and earnings could support a recovery

Despite the recent selloff, Nvidia shares trade at less than 12 times estimated earnings for the next 12 months, according to Barron's analysis.

A modest improvement in its valuation multiple could therefore support a significant recovery.

The company's upcoming third-quarter earnings report on Tuesday could provide an important catalyst.

Investors will closely monitor whether Nvidia reiterates its forecast for 70% revenue growth in fiscal 2028.

Any confirmation could help restore confidence in its growth prospects.

Additional share buybacks could also support the stock if its valuation remains depressed.

XTB analyst Kathleen Brooks said Nvidia's upcoming results would be closely watched following Huang's resignation.

While Brooks expects another strong earnings report, with revenue potentially exceeding the $108 billion estimate, she said the company's forward guidance would be more important for determining the stock's direction.

Yorkville Ives also maintained a bullish view, arguing that Nvidia remains the clear leader in GPU chips for the AI industry, with an estimated two-to-three-year advantage over its nearest competitor.

The analysts believe the current valuation does not fully reflect the company's position and see Colette Kress as a credible leader during the transition.

Leadership uncertainty remains an overhang

The absence of an immediate permanent successor is another challenge for Nvidia shares.

Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress is viewed as a potential interim leader, although the company is expected to require technical leadership for its next phase of growth.

Potential successors mentioned in early speculation include Ian Buck, Nvidia's vice president of hyperscale and high-performance computing, and Arm Holdings CEO Rene Haas.

Yorkville Ives also identified Apple CEO Tim Cook as a possible outside candidate, describing him as a dark-horse option given Nvidia's importance to the broader US technology industry.

A clearer succession plan or announcement of a shortlist could help reduce uncertainty surrounding the company's future direction.

Morgan Stanley reiterated its overweight rating on Nvidia but lowered its price target to $267 from $300.

The firm acknowledged that Huang's resignation, the absence of an immediate permanent successor and China-related regulatory risks represent setbacks.

However, it maintained that Nvidia's underlying business remains strong and that the risk-reward profile is attractive even under more conservative assumptions.

China scrutiny and corporate culture pose risks

The biggest threat to Nvidia's recovery could come from further developments surrounding the controversy that led to Huang's departure.

Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent questioned on Friday whether Nvidia had a sufficiently robust system to prevent its chips from reaching China through intermediaries.

Speaking to CNBC, he said he expected the company's board to conduct a thorough investigation.

Huang has reportedly agreed to testify before Congress, where lawmakers are interested in determining whether his reported relationship with a suspected Chinese intelligence agent resulted in the transfer of intellectual property or advanced hardware to China.

Hendi Susanto, portfolio manager at Gabelli Funds, said the next developments could depend on the findings of investigations and the level of scrutiny from Washington, particularly concerning China and export controls.

Truist also downgraded Nvidia to hold from buy, citing concerns about the company's culture and the possibility that GPUs may have reached Chinese companies and government entities.

These concerns could affect future revenue prospects if they lead to tighter restrictions or additional regulatory action.

data.title: AMD falls 9%, Intel drops 6% as chip stocks slide on Friday
data.description:
AMD and Intel shares fell sharply on Friday as technology stocks came under pressure, with investors assessing inflation data and uncertainty surrounding Nvidia's leadership.

AMD shares plunged more than 9%, while Intel declined around 6%.

Nvidia shares also dropped 3%, contributing to broader market losses.

The S&P 500 fell around 0.73%, while the Nasdaq Composite declined over 1.2%.

Despite the selloff, analysts remain constructive on AMD's competitive position in the artificial intelligence (AI) chip market, pointing to its growing product portfolio, expanding data-center business and opportunities arising from Nvidia's leadership uncertainty.

Inflation data initially lifts equities before reversal

US equities initially moved higher after October's producer price index (PPI) report showed wholesale prices increasing 0.3% month over month, below the 0.4% increase expected by economists polled by Dow Jones.

However, the report also showed producer prices rising 6.5% year over year, marking the largest annual increase since November 2022.

The inflation figures added to an uncertain backdrop for technology stocks, which subsequently reversed their initial gains.

Nvidia's leadership uncertainty also remained in focus following reports surrounding the potential departure of CEO Jensen Huang.

The development raises questions about the company's strategic investments, including its $5 billion investment in Intel in September 2025.

Nvidia formed a partnership with Intel to integrate the latter's central processing units (CPUs) with its own graphics processing units (GPUs).

Based on Intel's Thursday closing price of $61.20, Nvidia's investment is now worth more than $13.14 billion.

Although the investment has generated substantial gains, Nvidia is not under immediate pressure to sell its stake.

A potential divestment could also attract scrutiny from the Trump administration, which views Intel as an important player in US semiconductor manufacturing.

Recent analyst calls on the company have been mixed. Bank of America, RBC Capital and Barclays all kept hold ratings on the stock in recent updates.

Bank of America slashed its target price from $100 to $80.

Analysts see AMD gaining ground against Nvidia

Despite AMD's share price decline, Seaport Research analyst Jay Goldberg sees the company as an increasingly credible competitor to Nvidia.

Speaking to CNBC on Friday, Goldberg said AMD now offers "formidable products" that compete more effectively with Nvidia.

Goldberg believes uncertainty surrounding Nvidia could accelerate efforts by customers to diversify their chip suppliers.

While he stopped short of suggesting that Nvidia had lost its dominant position, he argued that AMD had progressed beyond simply establishing a foothold in the market.

Prime Capital Financial CIO Will McGough also sees opportunities for AMD and Broadcom as Nvidia navigates its leadership transition.

Speaking to CNBC on Friday, McGough highlighted Anthropic's use of AMD chips and said the market was reassessing Nvidia's competitive advantage as alternative suppliers improve their offerings.

He also pointed to Alphabet's Google, Amazon, and Chinese chipmakers developing their own silicon, potentially creating additional competition for Nvidia while opening opportunities for AMD.

Data-center growth could support AMD's expansion

Counterpoint Research's latest analysis also highlighted AMD's growing position in the data-center market.

Counterpoint expects the data center segment to contribute more than 80% of AMD's revenue in 2027, with estimated data-center revenue reaching approximately $77 billion.

The firm also noted that AMD's fourth-quarter revenue guidance of around $17 billion was approximately $800 million above consensus estimates.

Data-center revenue is expected to increase around 50% sequentially.

Counterpoint expects AMD's server business to roughly double in 2027, while AI-related data-center revenue could more than double.

The research firm said AMD's current advantage over Intel in data centers primarily comes from AI GPUs and racks rather than CPUs.

However, it expects meaningful gains in x86 server market share in 2027.

AMD has also secured supply from Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company to support its projected expansion.

data.title: Why are Micron, SK Hynix, and SanDisk stocks falling on Friday?
data.description:
Memory stocks including Micron, SK Hynix and SanDisk suffered losses on Friday as continued weakness in Nvidia weighed on semiconductor shares and intensified concerns about the sustainability of the artificial intelligence trade.

Micron MU and SK Hynix fell around 5% each, while SanDisk plunged 8%.

Nvidia slipped more than 4%, dragging the Philadelphia Semiconductor Index down over 5%.

The losses were considerably steeper than those in the broader market, with the Nasdaq falling 1.4% and the S&P 500 losing nearly 0.8%.

The selloff came even as October's producer price index (PPI) data came in softer than expected.

However, headline PPI accelerated 6.5% annually, up 0.2 percentage points and marking its highest annual rate since November 2022.

Nvidia uncertainty spills over into memory stocks

The turmoil surrounding Nvidia has raised questions about the broader AI trade, given the chipmaker's central role in the industry's expansion and its financial relationships with several companies across the ecosystem.

Investors are increasingly weighing concerns about AI infrastructure spending, debt financing, and the returns on massive capital investments.

Prolonged uncertainty around Nvidia could put additional pressure on valuations across the semiconductor sector.

China adds another layer of uncertainty.

Tighter US restrictions on advanced chips could accelerate domestic semiconductor substitution while making it harder for Chinese cloud companies to access sophisticated computing technology.

Memory stocks were already under pressure before Friday's decline.

Micron has lost around 21% over the past month, while SK Hynix is down approximately 18%.

The stocks also suffered a sell-off following Democratic victories in both houses of Congress, amid concerns that the political outcome could slow data centre construction across the US.

According to Charu Chanana, chief investment strategist at Saxo, further trouble at Nvidia could particularly affect SK Hynix and Micron.

SK Hynix's leading position as a supplier of high-bandwidth memory (HBM) for Nvidia leaves it exposed to potential disruptions in the chipmaker's product roadmap.

However, demand for advanced memory from other AI platforms could remain strong, providing some support to the stock.

For Micron, Nvidia-related delays could affect near-term demand expectations for advanced memory.

Nevertheless, competing AI accelerator platforms also require high-performance memory, which could help cushion the impact.

SanDisk faces additional NAND pricing concerns

SanDisk suffered a steeper decline, with shares falling 8% on Friday and losing more than 42% over the past month.

The latest pressure followed a warning from Kioxia about a potential surge in NAND flash prices, raising fresh questions about competitive pricing dynamics and the sustainability of SanDisk's elevated gross margins.

Also, the company's data centre business, which generated the bulk of its recent revenue growth, is heavily dependent on AI infrastructure spending linked to Nvidia's GPU ecosystem.

Any perceived threat to Nvidia's strategic continuity could therefore translate into uncertainty over future NAND flash demand.

However, Evercore ISI remains optimistic about SanDisk's longer-term prospects.

The brokerage reiterated its Outperform rating and $2,500 price target on Wednesday, arguing that investors are underestimating structural changes in the memory chipmaker's business.

The firm held investor meetings with CEO David Goeckeler and head of investor relations Ivan Donaldson over the past two days.

“We think investors remain overly focused on how long NAND pricing can stay elevated rather than appreciating the structural changes to SNDK’s model,” Evercore wrote.

Management sees a changing NAND market in which suppliers manage output to match demand rather than simply maximise production.

Price increases have now lasted around six quarters, compared with roughly two quarters historically.

Gross margins above 80% also reduce suppliers' incentive to chase market share.

Evercore believes SanDisk's multi-year supply agreements, which include committed demand, price floors and ceilings, and financial guarantees, could limit downside risks during a future downturn.

The brokerage also said data centre demand remained robust, with customers seeking additional supply for AI systems being deployed now.

A shift towards more durable, specialised memory could further tighten industry supply.

“NBMs + supply discipline should support more durable profitability, while AI demand + HBF provide incremental growth opportunities,” the firm said.

data.title: Is AI Mode killing the internet’s search-based business model?
data.description:
When AI chatbots burst onto the scene, there was chatter that they would kill Google search and the surrounding business models. 

The latest fiscal results are shedding some light on this prediction, and it seems that it is indeed affecting publishers and companies depending on Google search traffic. 

Google, in a bid to stay ahead of chatbots like ChatGPT and Claude, launched its own AI mode. 

However, that is creating another problem, as more users use AI mode instead of visiting the websites providing the information. 

There was a simple business model. Google crawled and indexed websites and displayed those links to users and directed traffic towards publishers. 

Those visits provided advertising revenue, attracted subscribers for higher-value information and allowed websites to build audiences. 

Artificial intelligence is challenging this model. 

Google’s AI Overviews and AI Mode provide users with information directly on search-result pages, reducing the need to click through to individual websites. 

The consequences are beginning to appear in company earnings.

Reddit reported a sharp decline in search referrals.

Freelance platform Fiverr also highlighted the impact of AI-related disruption on traditional search engine optimisation (SEO) work. 

Google is also facing challenges in generating advertising revenue from AI mode compared to revenue from conventional search.

The development raises a broader question about the sustainability of the open internet. 

If websites lose the traffic that finances their content, what happens to the information that AI models themselves depend on?

Industry executives believe the shift could represent a lasting change in the economics of the internet, with implications for publishers, companies and users. 

Google’s AI transformation is changing the economics of search

Google started AI Mode as an answer to ChatGPT.

ChatGPT’s introduction made companies question whether conversational AI would eventually replace a search engine.

The initiatives appear to be generating greater engagement. 

Google reported its highest query growth in five years. 

However, increased search activity does not necessarily translate into higher traffic for websites or greater advertising revenue for Google.

Alphabet’s third-quarter results highlighted this. 

The company reported search growth of 12%, down from 19% at the beginning of the year, while search and advertising revenue fell short of Wall Street expectations.

Google also warned of further pressure on search-revenue growth in the fourth quarter.

Another indication of the changing economics is the deceleration in paid-click growth. 

Google’s paid clicks increased 13% year over year in the first quarter, but the growth rate slowed to 8% in the third quarter.

AI Mode could be contributing to this shift.

Unlike conventional search, where users typically encounter several links and advertisements before visiting a website, AI Mode attempts to provide a more comprehensive response within Google's own interface.

This creates a different user experience. Consumers can ask follow-up questions, compare information, and explore topics without necessarily leaving Google.

For the search giant, the challenge is converting that engagement into revenue. 

For publishers, the problem is users tend to stay with Google’s AI Mode and end up not visiting their sites. 

Philipp Schindler, Google's chief business officer, acknowledged during the company's earnings call that AI Mode currently generates lower monetisation than traditional search, despite recording more queries.

Google is attempting to address the issue by expanding advertisements in AI Mode to additional countries and experimenting with new advertising placements as conversations progress.

Reddit's traffic decline offers an early warning

The consequences of this changing relationship are becoming particularly visible among websites that have historically depended on Google for audience acquisition.

Reddit is one of the clearest examples.

The platform's shares plunged approximately 29% on October 30 after its third-quarter results and outlook disappointed investors.

Investors were particularly concerned about weaker-than-expected user growth and the deterioration in search referrals.

Reddit CEO Steve Huffman said search traffic had declined by more than one million referrals per week during October.

He also warned that daily active users coming from search could decline by more than 10% in the fourth quarter.

Huffman suggested that Google's AI Overviews were becoming a more prominent part of the search experience, pushing traditional website links further down the results page.

“What started as a feature is now the full search experience,” he said during the earnings call. “And, at a minimum, it pushes everyone down the search page. And then, on top of that, the experiences themselves are not traffic drivers.”

He added that users continued to want Reddit's content, but Google was no longer directing visitors to the platform at the same rate.

"Google is crawling us as hard as ever, so the demand hasn't changed from their point of view either. The reality is, the AI mode does not drive traffic, not for us and not to anybody," Huffman said on the post-earnings call.

The distinction is important because Reddit's business model benefits from user engagement, conversations, and the extensive archive of discussions available on its platform.

Historically, Google helped introduce new users to those discussions. 

AI-generated answers can now provide information extracted from similar conversations without requiring users to visit Reddit.

The platform is responding by tightening access to its content. 

Reddit said it would begin trialling a requirement for users to log in to access the website in international markets before the end of the year.

The move is intended partly to restrict AI bots from scraping its content.

Publishers face a weakening incentive to produce free content

The problem extends beyond Reddit.

Fiverr CEO Micha Kaufman described the changes as an earthquake across the internet, arguing that organic clicks were declining as more consumers turned to AI assistants to find information.

“The internet as we’ve known it for the past 20-plus years is going away, and it’s going to completely change,” Kaufman said. “It’s dying.”

Fiverr's third-quarter revenue declined 15.8% from the year-earlier period.

In its shareholder letter, the company highlighted the impact of AI-related disruption on traditional SEO services, saying the changes had affected both low-value and high-end work on its platform.

The development could have broader consequences for digital publishing.

Many online businesses depend on organic search traffic to attract readers and generate advertising impressions. 

Others use search referrals to acquire customers, promote subscriptions or direct visitors towards commercial products.

When AI-generated summaries answer questions directly, fewer users may reach the original websites.

Monica Tartau, Head of Marketing at Aurora Labs, believes this represents a structural rather than temporary change.

“It looks more permanent than temporary to me,” Tartau told Invezz.

She argued that the traditional relationship between Google and publishers is changing because the search engine increasingly answers questions itself rather than directing users to the websites providing the underlying information.

Expert view

Google used to send people to websites. Now it answers the question itself (AI Mode & AI Overview) and keeps them there. It still needs the web for material, but it doesn’t need to send users to it the same way.

Head of Marketing at Aurora Labs
Monica Tartau

According to Tartau, this weakens the financial incentive for websites to continue producing freely accessible information.

“A lot of sites made money or justified the work because people clicked through from Google,” she said.

The expert added that when AI mode provides the answer before the user clicks, “that page view, ad, signup, or sale often doesn’t happen.”

The problem is particularly relevant for businesses that rely on large volumes of relatively inexpensive content and organic search traffic.

AI search could undermine the information it depends on

The potential consequences extend beyond the immediate financial pressure on publishers.

AI search engines rely on information produced across the internet. 

News organisations, specialist publications, research platforms and independent websites contribute material that helps AI systems answer questions.

If those publishers lose the revenue that finances their work, the supply of original information could deteriorate.

Michael Heinrich, CEO of 0G, described this as one of the more serious long-term risks associated with AI-powered search.

“Producing original information costs money,” Heinrich told Invezz.

Expert view

Whether you're running a newsroom, conducting scientific research or publishing specialist industry analysis, someone has to fund the work. If AI systems consume that information while reducing the audience publishers can monetize, eventually the economics stop making sense for some of them

CEO of 0G
Michael Heinrich

. 

Heinrich expects publishers to respond in different ways. 

“Larger publishers can negotiate licensing agreements, specialist platforms may move behind paywalls, and smaller independent sites could simply publish less,” the expert noted.

That creates a potential feedback loop.

“The problem for AI companies is that they still need a steady supply of accurate, current information. If fewer people are producing original material, AI systems risk drawing from an increasingly repetitive pool of secondary content, including material generated by other AI systems.”

This creates a contradiction for the AI industry. 

The technology could become increasingly effective at extracting and presenting information while simultaneously weakening the financial incentives that encourage people to produce that information in the first place.

Can Google make AI Mode as profitable as traditional search?

If Google backs AI Mode, it needs to find a way to transfer the advertising economics from search to AI Mode. 

In traditional search, a user searching for a particular product or a service can see sponsored links alongside organic results. 

Advertisers can compete for those placements, while Google earns revenue from commercial interactions.

AI Mode offers a different opportunity.

Because users can provide more context and ask follow-up questions, the platform may gain a better understanding of their needs and purchasing intentions.

Heinrich believes this could eventually create new advertising opportunities.

“If a user asks an AI assistant to compare laptops for a particular budget, for example, there's a very clear commercial intent that advertisers would be willing to pay to reach,” he said.

Google has already begun expanding advertisements within AI Mode, including to additional countries and through experiments involving advertisements that appear as conversations continue.

However, integrating advertising into AI-generated answers introduces another challenge: maintaining user trust.

In conventional search, sponsored links are generally distinguishable from organic results. 

Within a conversational AI response, the distinction between an objective recommendation and a paid placement could become less obvious.

Heinrich expects advertising decisions to continue reflecting user intent, relevance, conversion potential and advertiser bids.

But he cautioned that commercial incentives should not determine what an AI system presents as factual information.

If consumers begin questioning whether recommendations are genuinely useful or simply favour advertisers, Google could undermine the credibility of the product it is trying to monetise.

Tartau also noted that Google is already expanding advertisements in AI Mode, but said the company has acknowledged that these placements currently generate less revenue than conventional search advertisements.

She said Google's expectation is that users conducting early-stage research may become more commercially valuable as they continue asking follow-up questions.

For now, however, the ability to generate more interactions has not necessarily translated into equivalent monetisation.

Are paywalls and login requirements a good solution?

As search traffic becomes less reliable, websites are likely to reconsider how they distribute their content.

One option is restricting access through subscriptions, registration requirements, or other forms of login barriers.

Reddit is already planning this. By limiting access, the platform will make it more difficult for AI systems to scrape its discussions. 

Tartau said that for Reddit, “a login stops some of that, gives them a direct relationship with users, and more control.”

However, login requirements are not necessarily an effective solution for every publisher.

Tartau said such restrictions could also prevent casual visitors from discovering a website through search.

For Reddit, the strategy may make sense because its value lies partly in its extensive archive of conversations and user-generated discussions.

For a conventional publisher, the calculation is different.

“But if your business depends heavily on people discovering you through Google, putting everything behind a login can be quite damaging. You're effectively asking people to commit to your platform before they've had an opportunity to understand its value”, Heinrich added.

Experts expect many websites to adopt a middle-ground approach.

Michael Heinrich said there would be a hybrid approach where “publishers keep enough content publicly accessible to attract new readers while protecting premium research, proprietary data or specialist analysis.”

He believes publishers with differentiated content and established audiences could have greater opportunities to negotiate licensing agreements with AI companies.

However, smaller websites that depend heavily on search discovery could face greater difficulties.

The expert also highlighted an important distinction: restricting access through a login wall does not automatically establish ownership rights or prevent every form of AI use.

He added that a publisher's negotiating position will depend on the uniqueness of its information, licensing arrangements and the technical controls used to enforce access.

“Most sites will probably do something in the middle: leave some stuff open so they can still be found, put the better material or tools behind a login, and try to build more direct relationships through newsletters and apps so they’re less dependent on Google,” Monica Tartau added. 

The internet's next business model remains uncertain

Despite the hybrid model’s possibility, there is still uncertainty for the publishers. 

Funding the content that populates the internet is always a challenge. Free information was supported by advertisements driven through clicks. 

As AI models eat up advertisements and clicks, it threatens to close off the internet and make users pay for basic access. 

Key takeaway

The open web only works if someone is still willing to fund the content that lives on it.

Head of Marketing at Aurora Labs
Monica Tartau

The internet's search-based business model is therefore facing more than a decline in clicks. 

It is confronting a fundamental question about who gets paid when information is created, indexed, extracted, and delivered through artificial intelligence.

data.title: Apple stock gains as Bernstein highlights safe-haven appeal amid AI selloff
data.description:
Apple shares rose 0.99% on Friday, even as broader technology stocks came under pressure following Nvidia's decline.

The iPhone maker is increasingly attracting investors seeking exposure to a relatively defensive technology business amid uncertainty surrounding artificial intelligence (AI) stocks, according to Bernstein analysts.

In a report published Thursday, Bernstein analysts led by Mark Newman said Apple had become less correlated with its large-cap technology peers and was increasingly trading alongside high-quality consumer companies.

"With little correlation to tech peers, Apple now trades in line with high quality consumer stocks," the analysts said.

The assessment comes as Nvidia faces leadership uncertainty following reports surrounding CEO Jensen Huang, while concerns about the substantial capital expenditure requirements of AI infrastructure continue to weigh on technology stocks.

Apple gains safe-haven appeal as AI spending weighs on tech

Unlike several other Magnificent Seven companies, Apple has relatively modest capital expenditure requirements.

Its capital expenditure accounts for less than 2% of revenue, compared with the hundreds of billions of dollars being committed by major technology companies to AI infrastructure.

Bernstein described Apple as a consumer compounder, noting that its revenue growth, earnings generation and free cash flow profile increasingly resemble those of established consumer businesses.

The brokerage reiterated its outperform rating on Apple and maintained a $380 price target, implying approximately 7% upside from Thursday's closing price.

Apple trades at around 37 times its expected earnings per share for 2027, roughly twice the broader market's forward earnings multiple.

Among companies with market capitalizations above $200 billion and expected EPS growth below 15%, only Costco, Walmart and General Electric also trade at forward price-to-earnings multiples above 30.

However, Apple's projected annual revenue growth through 2029 is approximately 9%, compared with 7% for Costco and 5% for Walmart.

Bernstein also highlighted Apple's estimated 3.1% free cash flow yield and expected share repurchases equivalent to 3% of its market capitalization in 2027 and 3.2% in 2028.

iPhone demand and services offer growth opportunities

Apple's operating performance continues to provide support for its valuation.

In the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026, iPhone revenue increased 17% year over year to $57.6 billion, despite supply constraints.

The company reported September-quarter revenue records for iPhone and record upgrades worldwide, including in the US, China and India.

The launch of iPhone Duo, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max, has expanded its product portfolio and created additional upgrade opportunities.

AI also represents a potential growth driver.

Apple's planned improvements to Siri, including personalized assistance and contextual awareness, could encourage customers to upgrade to newer devices.

The company may also generate additional revenue by offering expanded access to advanced server-based AI capabilities.

Its Services business provides another monetization opportunity.

With more than 2.5 billion active devices worldwide, Apple has a substantial installed base for services such as Apple Pay, iCloud+, Apple Music and Apple TV.

The expansion of bundled services and the introduction of Apple Pay in India and advertising on Apple Maps could support further growth.

Rising memory costs and supply constraints pose risks

Despite its defensive characteristics, Apple faces several operational challenges.

The company expects gross margin to decline to 45%-46% in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, compared with 47.9% in the fourth quarter of fiscal 2026.

Rising memory prices and expenses related to Siri AI are expected to contribute to the decline.

Apple also continues to face supply constraints involving advanced semiconductor manufacturing capacity and memory components.

While advanced-node constraints are easing, memory shortages could affect Mac and iPad availability during the December quarter.

Regulatory scrutiny of its App Store business model and third-party licensing arrangements presents another risk.

Apple expects Services revenue growth to moderate to 8%-9% in the first quarter of fiscal 2027, compared with 10% in the preceding quarter, partly reflecting licensing-related and foreign-exchange headwinds.

These pressures could test Apple's ability to sustain its premium valuation even as investors increasingly view the company as a defensive alternative within the technology sector.

data.title: What is ChatGPT Wallet, how does it work and who can use it?
data.description:
OpenAI has given its AI agents a way to pay. ChatGPT Wallet, unveiled on Friday, lets the company’s “dots” agents complete purchases for users, provided the user signs off on each one.

OpenAI set out the details in a blog post and a help-centre guide.

Built with American Express, Mastercard and Visa, the feature starts small, but it is OpenAI’s second attempt in just over a year to take ChatGPT from product research to the checkout.

What is ChatGPT Wallet?

ChatGPT Wallet is a payment feature inside dots, the always-on personal agents OpenAI unveiled at its DevDay conference on 29 September.

Until now, a dot that found a sweater or a hotel room still needed a human to finish checkout. With Wallet, users save a card once, and the agent pays through the merchant’s normal checkout.

Cards saved in Wallet are kept separate from the one that pays for the ChatGPT subscription, and from any prepaid ChatGPT balance.

How does ChatGPT Wallet work?

OpenAI’s guidance describes five stages. The user adds a card through a secure form rather than in the chat, and the bank may ask for verification. The user then asks their dot to find something, such as a hotel for a weekend trip.

Before paying, the dot shows the merchant, items, total, chosen card and any recurring-payment terms. The user approves with a biometric check such as Face ID or Touch ID, creating a record of what was authorised.

Finally, the card network issues a payment token, a substitute card number, security code and expiry date, which the agent enters at checkout. The real card details are never shared with the agent or the merchant, OpenAI says.

OpenAI is not taking a fee on transactions at launch, according to CNBC. The sale is between shopper and merchant, which keeps control of pricing, delivery and returns.

Who can use ChatGPT Wallet?

Wallet is open only to ChatGPT Pro subscribers, whose plans cost $100 to $500 a month. Users must be 18 or over, live in the US and hold an eligible US-issued card with a US billing address. It works only in conversations with a dot.

OpenAI’s help centre lists eligible Chase cards for primary cardholders, alongside Amex, Mastercard and Visa. Virtual cards are not supported at launch.

There is no timetable for Free, Go or Plus users, or for the UK and Europe. Amex’s Luke Gebb told CNBC the narrow rollout was deliberate.

What does it mean for consumers?

The main gain is convenience: an agent can take a purchase from search to payment without the user retyping card details.

OpenAI says shoppers keep their card rewards and protections for eligible disputes, such as a faulty item. Refunds go through the merchant, and unrecognised charges through the card issuer.

There are drawbacks. OpenAI concedes some sites may block agents or flag their purchases as fraud. Amazon stops agents buying on its platform, CNBC reported, and United Airlines said this week it would block third-party AI agents from booking. OpenAI also tells users that a “ready to check out” message does not confirm an order.

Privacy is another consideration. Merchants may still need a name, phone number, email and delivery address, which can be passed on through the conversation.

Longer term, OpenAI wants users to pre-approve purchases within spending limits, categories or time windows, so the agent need not ask each time. It has given no date for that.

Why is OpenAI doing this?

OpenAI says 1.2 billion people use ChatGPT each week, many of them to research what to buy, and it had nearly 100 million paying users at the end of the third quarter, CNBC reported.

Its first checkout push stalled. Instant Checkout, launched in September 2025 with the Agentic Commerce Protocol built alongside Stripe, was wound down in March, when OpenAI said it lacked flexibility for merchants.

Wallet takes a different route, using merchants’ existing checkouts and the card networks’ token systems. OpenAI is also working with payment firms including Stripe and Adyen, and fraud-prevention specialists such as Forter and Signifyd, so genuine agent purchases are not wrongly declined.

How have markets reacted?

OpenAI is privately held, so attention turned to its listed partners.

At 16:55 GMT, Visa was up 1.4% at $426.20 and Mastercard 1.4% at $661.46 against Thursday’s close, while Amex was 0.5% higher at $319.77, according to Yahoo Finance data.

The moves are modest and cannot be pinned on the launch alone.

What happens next?

OpenAI has published a Commerce Partner Playbook showing merchants how to let its agents through and share product feeds. It says it will widen access once it has learned from early use with businesses, banks and card networks.

data.title: Kraken owner Payward’s Q3 adjusted EBITDA falls 67% as trading volumes slide
data.description:
Payward, the parent company of crypto exchange Kraken, reported a sharp fall in third-quarter profit from a year earlier, even as results recovered from a weak second quarter.

In its Q3 2026 financial highlights, published on Friday, November 13, the company said adjusted EBITDA was $60 million, up from $23 million in the second quarter. Bloomberg, which reviewed Payward’s shareholder letter, reported that the figure was down 67% year on year.

Payward also changed how it reports. It now uses Total Platform Margin (TPM) in place of adjusted revenue, deducting both the cost of crypto delivered to clients and the staking rewards it pays out. On that basis TPM was $487 million, up 12% from $436 million in Q2 and down 12% from a year earlier.

Volumes down on the year, up on the quarter

Total platform transaction volume was $353 billion, which Payward said was 22% higher than in Q2 but 30% lower than in Q3 2025.

The company said it grew while industry spot volume fell 7% quarter on quarter, citing CoinMarketCap data, and that its share of industry spot volume rose to 6.5% in September from 3.3% a year earlier.

Bloomberg linked the annual decline to softer crypto prices. Bitcoin rallied roughly 40% from mid-August to early October before retreating on inflation worries and concern over how the US midterm elections could affect the industry. Exchanges that depend on trading fees tend to see activity slow when prices fall.

Average assets on platform were $43 billion, down 21% year on year. Payward said that at constant prices they rose 29% to $71 billion, and that clients had added assets in each of the last 12 months.

Less reliance on trading fees

The company is trying to show that its business is no longer just about spot trading. It split TPM into three buckets for the first time:

  • transaction-based TPM rose 7% quarter on quarter to $234 million;
  • asset-based TPM, earned on assets clients hold, rose 26% to $128 million;
  • access-based TPM, from subscriptions, trader evaluations, listings and index licences, rose 7% to $125 million.

Asset- and access-based income together made up 52% of the total, up from 46% a year earlier. Derivatives contracts traded rose 84% year on year to 66 million, billable accounts rose 74% to 1.5 million, and funded accounts rose 37% to 7.1 million. Payward notes that funded accounts are not a count of unique clients, as one client can hold several.

Tokenised stocks, banking and AI agents

Payward said its xStocks tokenised equities business passed $1 billion in assets under management in October and now offers more than 700 tokenised stocks. Earlier this week it added hundreds of UK and EU-listed shares, including the DAX 40.

In the US it plans to offer onchain perpetual futures, starting on Hyperliquid, and single-stock perpetual futures, both subject to regulatory approval. Prediction markets for US clients are listed as a next step, though the company gave no timing. In October it agreed to buy Saldo Bank, an EU-licensed digital bank, with completion subject to regulatory approval.

Payward also named AI as a fifth business pillar alongside trading, banking, asset management and Payward Services. It said every Payward app will get an “agent harness” through which clients can direct AI agents across their holdings, with the first expected early next year. It also plans to launch a personal finance agent, designed to act only within client-set limits and with client approval before a trade runs.

On regulation, Payward said Kraken plans to launch in the UAE following full market approval from Dubai’s Virtual Assets Regulatory Authority (VARA), and that it has received in-principle approval from Kazakhstan’s AFSA.

Bloomberg has previously reported that Payward’s initial public offering may not happen until next year.

For more on the exchange’s fees, products and licences, see our Kraken review. Readers comparing platforms can also check our guide to the best crypto exchanges.

data.title: It's not just Nvidia, IonQ stock is also slipping on leadership shake-up
data.description:
Nvidia isn’t the only technology company facing investor scrutiny over a leadership change.

IonQ (IONQ) stock tanked on November 13 after the quantum computing company announced an immediate executive departure and a reshuffle of its finance team.

The disclosure brings uncertainty just over a week after IONQ raised its revenue outlook – leaving investors weighing fast commercial expansion against management shake-up and the considerable cost of building the business.

Why finance team reshuffle is hurting IonQ stock

In its press release, IonQ said CFO Inder Singh is stepping down immediately, and Gary Merril – the current chief of finance at Commvault – will replace him in early December.

The company also appointed former Juniper Networks’ senior executive Thomas Austin to a newly created chief accounting officer position.

The bearish implication is uncertainty over financial leadership during an expansion that requires careful spending and acquisition integration.

An abrupt transition can make investors demand stronger evidence that execution remains on track.

However, the appointments alone provide no basis for concluding that IonQ Inc faces accounting problems.

Experienced replacements may ultimately strengthen oversight as the business grows.

In short, the sell-off in IONQ stock today reflects uncertainty; where that uncertainty becomes a lasting concern depends on what the incoming team delivers.

Is it worth buying the dip in IONQ shares today?

IonQ shares retain a credible growth case.

The company reported Q3 sales of nearly $174 million, up a whopping 336% year-on-year, and raised its 2026 guidance to $505 million at least.

That said, investors must examine the composition: acquired foundry SkyWater contributed $83.5 million, nearly half the quarterly sales total.

IonQ’s platform segment separately grew a whopping 127% to $90.3 million.

That distinction matters when valuing the stock.

Buying a larger revenue base does not establish how quickly existing operations can expand – or how profitable the combined company will become.

The latest quarter also included a $133.6 million adjusted EBITDA loss.

So IonQ Inc may interest investors comfortable with substantial execution risk, but a lower share price alone doesn’t establish a bargain.

What investors should watch before calling a bottom

IonQ has financial resources to support its ambitions.

It reported $1.7 billion in cash, equivalents and investments at September 30, rising to $3.7 billion on a pro forma basis after October’s $2 billion equity offering.

That financing provides flexibility, although issuing shares dilutes existing ownership.

For prospective buyers, the more useful signals are continued platform growth, progress toward lower operating losses and disciplined integration of acquired businesses.

Clear communication from the incoming finance team would also help investors assess spending priorities.

What’s also worth mentioning is that today’s decline in IONQ shares coincides with weakness in quantum computing stocks at large, so the leadership announcement doesn’t explain every percentage point lost.

IonQ’s challenge is to demonstrate that its expanding business can create durable shareholder value alongside impressive revenue growth.
